title: NORCET — Pharmacology | Drug Antagonism
description: Subject-wise test on Drug Antagonism (Pharmacology) for NORCET. 25Q.

questions.question: A 28-year-old male with hypertension is prescribed a drug that selectively blocks angiotensin II receptors on vascular smooth muscle. Which type of antagonism is this drug exhibiting?

options.explanation: Competitive antagonism involves reversible binding to the same receptor as the agonist, which is not the case here.
Non-competitive antagonism involves irreversible binding or binding to an allosteric site, reducing the maximal response.
Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs produce opposing physiological effects, such as blocking angiotensin II receptors while the body compensates through other mechanisms.
Chemical antagonism involves direct chemical interaction between two drugs, such as inactivation of one drug by another.

questions.explanation: Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs act on different receptors or mechanisms to produce opposite effects, counteracting each other's actions. Here, the drug blocks angiotensin II receptors, reducing its vasoconstrictive effects, while the body may compensate through other mechanisms (e.g., increased sympathetic output).
questions.hint: Consider the mechanism of angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) and their impact on vascular smooth muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following is the defining characteristic of a non-competitive antagonist?

options.text: It binds reversibly to the same site as the agonist
options.explanation: This describes competitive antagonism, not non-competitive.

options.text: It reduces the maximal response of the agonist even at high concentrations
options.explanation: This is the defining characteristic of a non-competitive antagonist, as it prevents the agonist from achieving maximal effect.

options.text: It shifts the dose-response curve to the right without changing the maximal response
options.explanation: This describes competitive antagonism, which shifts the curve rightward but does not reduce Emax.

options.text: It chemically inactivates the agonist before it reaches the receptor
options.explanation: Chemical antagonism involves direct chemical interaction, which is not the defining feature of non-competitive antagonism.

questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists bind to a site other than the agonist's binding site (allosteric site) or irreversibly to the agonist's site, preventing the agonist from fully activating the receptor. This reduces the maximal response (Emax) of the agonist, even at high concentrations.
questions.hint: Think about how non-competitive antagonists affect the dose-response curve.
questions.subject: norcet-pharmacology

questions.question: A patient is given a drug that binds to the muscarinic acetylcholine receptors and prevents acetylcholine from binding. Which type of antagonism is this?

options.explanation: Atropine is a classic example of a competitive antagonist at muscarinic receptors.
Irreversible antagonism involves permanent binding, which is not the case here.
Functional antagonism involves opposing physiological effects, not direct receptor blockade.
Pharmacokinetic antagonism involves altering drug absorption or metabolism, not receptor binding.

questions.explanation: Competitive antagonism occurs when the antagonist binds reversibly to the same receptor as the agonist, competing for binding. This can be overcome by increasing the agonist concentration.
questions.hint: Consider how atropine works on muscarinic receptors.

questions.question: The dose-response curve for drug X shifts to the right in the presence of drug Y, but the maximal response remains unchanged. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Drug Y is a non-competitive antagonist
options.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists reduce Emax, which is not observed here.

options.text: Drug Y is an irreversible antagonist
options.explanation: Irreversible antagonists also reduce Emax.

options.text: Drug Y is a competitive antagonist
options.explanation: Competitive antagonists shift the curve rightward without reducing Emax.

options.text: Drug Y is a chemical antagonist
options.explanation: Chemical antagonists involve direct chemical interaction, not receptor competition.

questions.explanation: A rightward shift in the dose-response curve with no change in the maximal response (Emax) indicates competitive antagonism. The antagonist (drug Y) competes with the agonist (drug X) for the same receptor.
questions.hint: Think about how competitive antagonists affect the dose-response curve.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of drugs demonstrates chemical antagonism?

options.explanation: Propranolol is a competitive antagonist of epinephrine at beta-adrenergic receptors, but this is not chemical antagonism.
Protamine sulfate chemically binds to and inactivates heparin, demonstrating chemical antagonism.
Naloxone is a competitive antagonist of morphine at opioid receptors, not chemical antagonism.
Atropine is a competitive antagonist of acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, not chemical antagonism.

questions.explanation: Chemical antagonism occurs when two drugs combine in solution, resulting in the inactivation of one or both drugs. Protamine sulfate (a positively charged protein) chemically binds to and inactivates heparin (a negatively charged anticoagulant).
questions.hint: Consider examples where drugs directly neutralize each other chemically.
questions.subject: norcet-pharmacology

questions.question: A researcher is studying a new drug that binds irreversibly to the active site of an enzyme, reducing its activity by 80% even at high substrate concentrations. Which type of antagonism does this drug exhibit?

options.explanation: Competitive antagonists do not reduce Emax; they only shift the curve rightward.
Non-competitive antagonists reduce Emax by irreversibly binding to the enzyme's active site.
Functional antagonism involves opposing physiological effects, not direct enzyme inhibition.
Pharmacokinetic antagonism involves altering drug metabolism or excretion, not direct enzyme inhibition.

questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonism involves irreversible binding to the receptor or an allosteric site, leading to a reduction in the maximal response (Emax) of the agonist. Here, the drug reduces enzyme activity by 80% even at high substrate concentrations.
questions.hint: Consider how irreversible binding affects enzyme activity and the dose-response relationship.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about functional antagonism is correct?

options.text: It involves direct binding of the antagonist to the agonist
options.explanation: Functional antagonism does not involve direct binding; it involves opposing physiological effects.

options.text: It always results in a shift of the dose-response curve to the right
options.explanation: Functional antagonism does not necessarily shift the dose-response curve; it involves opposing effects.

options.text: It occurs when two drugs produce opposing physiological effects
options.explanation: This is the defining characteristic of functional antagonism.

options.text: It is a type of chemical antagonism where the antagonist inactivates the agonist
options.explanation: Chemical antagonism involves direct chemical interaction, not opposing physiological effects.

questions.explanation: Functional antagonism (also called physiological antagonism) occurs when two drugs act on different receptors or pathways to produce opposite effects, counteracting each other.
questions.hint: Think about how histamine and epinephrine produce opposing effects.

questions.question: A patient is administered a drug that binds to the same receptor as the agonist but cannot activate it. Increasing the agonist concentration does not overcome the antagonism. Which type of antagonism is this?

options.explanation: Competitive antagonism is reversible and can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration.
Irreversible competitive antagonists bind permanently to the receptor, preventing agonist binding and activation.
Non-competitive antagonists bind to allosteric sites or irreversibly, but the key here is the same receptor binding.
Pharmacokinetic antagonism involves altering drug absorption or metabolism, not receptor binding.

questions.explanation: Irreversible competitive antagonism involves the antagonist binding irreversibly to the receptor, preventing the agonist from binding. Unlike reversible competitive antagonism, increasing the agonist concentration cannot overcome this blockade.
questions.hint: Consider how irreversible binding affects receptor activation and the ability to overcome antagonism.

questions.question: The graph below shows the dose-response curves for drug A alone and drug A in the presence of drug B. Which type of antagonism does drug B exhibit? (Assume the graph shows a rightward shift in the dose-response curve of drug A with no change in Emax)

options.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists reduce Emax, which is not observed in the graph.
Competitive antagonists shift the dose-response curve rightward without reducing Emax.
Functional antagonism involves opposing physiological effects, not a rightward shift in the curve.
Chemical antagonism involves direct chemical interaction, not a shift in the dose-response curve.

questions.explanation: The graph depicts a rightward shift in the dose-response curve of drug A without a change in the maximal response (Emax). This is characteristic of competitive antagonism, where the antagonist (drug B) competes with the agonist (drug A) for the same receptor.
questions.hint: Think about how competitive antagonists affect the dose-response curve visually.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of pharmacokinetic antagonism?

options.text: Naloxone reversing the effects of morphine by binding to opioid receptors
options.explanation: This is an example of competitive antagonism at opioid receptors.

options.text: Cholestyramine binding to bile acids in the gut, reducing their absorption
options.explanation: Cholestyramine alters the absorption of bile acids, demonstrating pharmacokinetic antagonism.

options.text: Propranolol blocking the effects of epinephrine by binding to beta-adrenergic receptors
options.explanation: This is an example of competitive antagonism at beta-adrenergic receptors.

options.text: Atropine blocking the effects of acetylcholine by binding to muscarinic receptors
options.explanation: This is an example of competitive antagonism at muscarinic receptors.

questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetic antagonism occurs when one drug alters the absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion of another drug, reducing its concentration or effect at the site of action. Cholestyramine binds to bile acids in the gut, preventing their reabsorption and reducing cholesterol levels.
questions.hint: Consider examples where one drug affects the pharmacokinetics of another.

questions.question: Which type of drug antagonism involves two drugs acting at the same receptor site but producing opposite effects?

options.explanation: Physiological antagonism involves drugs acting on different receptors or systems to produce opposing effects.
Pharmacological antagonism occurs when two drugs bind to the same receptor but produce opposite pharmacological effects.
Chemical antagonism involves drugs reacting chemically to neutralize each other's effects.
Pharmacokinetic antagonism involves drugs altering the absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion of another drug.

questions.explanation: Pharmacological antagonism occurs when two drugs bind to the same receptor but produce opposite pharmacological effects. This is the classic definition of drug antagonism at the receptor level.
questions.hint: Think about drugs acting on the same receptor but opposing each other's effects.
questions.subject: norcet-pharmacology

questions.question: A patient is receiving a beta-blocker for hypertension. The physician adds a beta-agonist to manage an acute asthmatic attack. This interaction is an example of:

options.explanation: Irreversible antagonism involves permanent binding of the antagonist to the receptor.
Non-competitive antagonism involves binding to a site other than the agonist binding site, reducing maximal response.
Uncompetitive antagonism requires prior activation of the receptor by the agonist before binding.
Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs produce opposing physiological effects, such as a beta-blocker and a beta-agonist.

questions.explanation: Functional antagonism (also called physiological antagonism) occurs when two drugs act on different receptors or systems but produce opposing physiological effects, balancing each other out.
questions.hint: Consider the opposing physiological effects of beta-blockers and beta-agonists.

questions.question: In a dose-response study, Drug X produces a 50% maximal response (ED50) at a dose of 10 mg. When Drug Y is administered prior to Drug X, the ED50 of Drug X shifts to 50 mg. What type of antagonism is most likely occurring?

options.explanation: Competitive reversible antagonism shifts the dose-response curve to the right but does not decrease maximal response.
Competitive irreversible antagonism shifts the dose-response curve to the right and decreases maximal response as receptors are permanently occupied.
Non-competitive antagonism reduces maximal response without shifting the dose-response curve.
Chemical antagonism involves chemical neutralization of the drug rather than receptor interaction.

questions.explanation: The shift in ED50 to a higher dose without a decrease in maximal response suggests irreversible antagonism, where the antagonist binds permanently to the receptor, reducing the number of available receptors for the agonist.
questions.hint: Look for a shift in the dose-response curve without a change in maximal efficacy.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the Schild plot used in pharmacology?

options.text: It is used to determine the efficacy of a non-competitive antagonist
options.explanation: The Schild plot is specifically used for competitive antagonism, not non-competitive.

options.text: It is used to analyze competitive antagonism by plotting log(dose ratio - 1) against log(antagonist concentration)
options.explanation: The Schild plot analyzes competitive antagonism by plotting log(dose ratio - 1) vs. log(antagonist concentration).

options.text: It helps measure the pKa of a drug
options.explanation: The Schild plot is not used to measure pKa.

options.text: It is used to determine the volume of distribution of a drug
options.explanation: The volume of distribution is determined by other pharmacokinetic methods.

questions.explanation: The Schild plot is a graphical method used to analyze competitive antagonism. It plots the logarithm of the dose ratio minus one against the logarithm of the antagonist concentration to determine antagonist potency.
questions.hint: Recall the purpose and axes of the Schild plot.

questions.question: A new drug candidate is being tested for its ability to inhibit the effects of acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors. The study shows that increasing concentrations of the drug reduce the maximal response of acetylcholine without shifting the dose-response curve. What type of antagonism does this drug exhibit?

options.explanation: Competitive reversible antagonism shifts the dose-response curve to the right without reducing maximal response.
Competitive irreversible antagonism shifts the dose-response curve to the right and reduces maximal response.
Non-competitive antagonism reduces maximal response without shifting the dose-response curve.
Physiological antagonism involves drugs acting on different systems to produce opposing effects.

questions.explanation: Non-competitive antagonism reduces the maximal response of the agonist without shifting the dose-response curve, indicating that the antagonist acts at a site other than the agonist binding site, or irreversibly binds to the receptor.
questions.hint: Look for a reduction in maximal response without a shift in the curve.

questions.question: A patient presents with an overdose of a cholinesterase inhibitor. The physician administers atropine to counteract the muscarinic effects. This interaction is an example of:

options.explanation: Competitive antagonism involves drugs binding to the same receptor site.
Non-competitive antagonism involves binding to a different site or irreversible binding.
Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs produce opposing physiological effects, such as atropine blocking muscarinic effects of excess acetylcholine.
Chemical antagonism involves chemical neutralization of the drug.

questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors while the cholinesterase inhibitor increases acetylcholine levels. This is functional antagonism because atropine and the cholinesterase inhibitor produce opposing physiological effects.
questions.hint: Atropine and cholinesterase inhibitors have opposing effects on muscarinic receptors.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of irreversible competitive antagonists?

options.text: They can be overcome by increasing the agonist concentration
options.explanation: Reversible competitive antagonists can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration, but irreversible ones cannot.

options.text: They cause a decrease in the maximal response of the agonist
options.explanation: Irreversible competitive antagonists reduce the number of available receptors, decreasing maximal response.

options.text: They do not bind to the receptor
options.explanation: Irreversible competitive antagonists do bind to the receptor but in a permanent manner.

options.text: They increase the efficacy of the agonist
options.explanation: Irreversible competitive antagonists decrease, not increase, the efficacy of the agonist.

questions.explanation: Irreversible competitive antagonists bind permanently to the receptor, reducing the number of available receptors and thus decreasing the maximal response of the agonist.
questions.hint: Irreversible antagonists permanently occupy receptors.

questions.question: A research study is conducted to determine the pA2 value of a competitive antagonist. The pA2 is defined as:

options.text: The negative logarithm of the agonist concentration that produces a 50% maximal response
options.explanation: This describes the pD2 value, not pA2.

options.text: The negative logarithm of the antagonist concentration that reduces the agonist's effect by half
options.explanation: The pA2 value is the negative logarithm of the antagonist concentration that requires a two-fold increase in agonist concentration.

options.text: The logarithm of the dose ratio minus one
options.explanation: This is a component of the Schild plot but not the definition of pA2.

options.text: The logarithm of the concentration of the agonist required to produce a 20% maximal response
options.explanation: This describes a different pharmacodynamic parameter.

questions.explanation: The pA2 value is the negative logarithm of the antagonist concentration that requires a two-fold increase in agonist concentration to produce the same effect as in the absence of the antagonist.
questions.hint: Recall that pA2 is related to the potency of a competitive antagonist.

questions.question: In a clinical scenario, a patient is given naloxone to reverse the respiratory depression caused by an opioid overdose. Naloxone acts by:

options.text: Increasing the metabolism of the opioid
options.explanation: Naloxone does not increase the metabolism of opioids.
Naloxone binds competitively, not irreversibly.
Naloxone competitively antagonizes opioid receptors, reversing their effects.
Naloxone does not chemically inactivate opioids.

questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at opioid receptors. It binds to the receptors and displaces the opioid, reversing its effects, including respiratory depression.
questions.hint: Naloxone is known to block opioid receptors competitively.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the dose-response curve in the presence of a non-competitive antagonist?

options.text: The curve shifts to the right with no change in the maximal response
options.explanation: This describes competitive antagonism, not non-competitive.

options.text: The curve shifts to the right with a decrease in the maximal response
options.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists do not shift the curve to the right.

options.text: The curve remains unchanged in position but shows a decrease in the maximal response
options.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists reduce maximal response without shifting the dose-response curve.

options.text: The curve shifts to the left with an increase in the maximal response
options.explanation: Non-competitive antagonists do not cause a left shift or increase maximal response.

questions.explanation: A non-competitive antagonist reduces the maximal response of the agonist by binding to an allosteric site or irreversibly binding to the receptor, but it does not shift the dose-response curve to the right.
questions.hint: Non-competitive antagonists affect maximal response rather than shifting the curve.

questions.question: A 55-year-old male with hypertension is prescribed a new antihypertensive drug. The drug’s mechanism involves blocking the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor, thereby preventing angiotensin II from exerting its vasoconstrictive effects. Which type of drug antagonism best describes this mechanism?

options.explanation: Competitive antagonism occurs when the antagonist binds to the same receptor site as the agonist, competing for binding.
Non-competitive antagonism occurs when the antagonist binds to a different site than the agonist, reducing the maximal response.
Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs have opposite effects on the same physiological function.
Chemical antagonism occurs when two drugs combine in solution, forming an inactive product.

questions.explanation: The drug blocks the AT1 receptor, preventing angiotensin II from binding and exerting its effect. This is a classic example of non-competitive antagonism, where the antagonist binds to a different site than the agonist, reducing the maximal response.
questions.hint: Consider whether the antagonist binds to the same site as the agonist or a different site.
questions.subject: norcet-pharmacology

questions.question: A researcher is studying the interaction between two drugs, Drug X and Drug Y. Drug X binds to the same receptor as the endogenous ligand but does not activate it, while Drug Y binds to a different site on the receptor and reduces its affinity for the endogenous ligand. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Drug X is a non-competitive antagonist, and Drug Y is a competitive antagonist.
options.explanation: This is incorrect because Drug X binds to the same site as the endogenous ligand, making it a competitive antagonist.

options.text: Drug X is a competitive antagonist, and Drug Y is a non-competitive antagonist.
options.explanation: Drug X binds to the same site as the endogenous ligand but does not activate it, making it a competitive antagonist. Drug Y binds to a different site and reduces the receptor’s affinity for the ligand, making it a non-competitive antagonist.

options.text: Both Drug X and Drug Y are competitive antagonists.
options.explanation: This is incorrect because Drug Y binds to a different site, making it a non-competitive antagonist.

options.text: Both Drug X and Drug Y are non-competitive antagonists.
options.explanation: This is incorrect because Drug X binds to the same site as the endogenous ligand, making it a competitive antagonist.

questions.explanation: Drug X binds to the same site as the endogenous ligand but does not activate it, making it a competitive antagonist. Drug Y binds to a different site and reduces the receptor’s affinity for the ligand, making it a non-competitive antagonist.
questions.hint: Consider the binding site and effect on receptor affinity for each drug.
questions.subject: norcet-pharmacology

questions.question: In a laboratory experiment, a researcher observes that Drug A reduces the effect of Drug B by binding to Drug B and forming an inactive complex. Which type of drug antagonism is demonstrated here?

options.explanation: Pharmacokinetic antagonism occurs when one drug alters the absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion of another drug.
Pharmacodynamic antagonism occurs when two drugs have opposing effects on the same physiological function.
Chemical antagonism occurs when two drugs combine in solution, forming an inactive product.
Physiological antagonism occurs when two drugs have opposite effects on the same physiological function.

questions.explanation: Chemical antagonism occurs when two drugs combine in solution, resulting in an inactive product. This directly reduces the effect of one of the drugs.
questions.hint: Consider whether the drugs combine chemically to form an inactive product.
questions.subject: norcet-pharmacology

questions.question: A patient with asthma is given a beta-2 agonist (e.g., albuterol) to relieve bronchospasm. However, the patient’s symptoms worsen because an unrecognized beta-blocker was inadvertently administered. Which type of antagonism explains this interaction?

options.explanation: Competitive antagonism occurs when the antagonist binds to the same receptor site as the agonist, competing for binding.
Non-competitive antagonism occurs when the antagonist binds to a different site than the agonist, reducing the maximal response.
Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs have opposite effects on the same physiological function.
Chemical antagonism occurs when two drugs combine in solution, forming an inactive product.

questions.explanation: Functional antagonism occurs when two drugs have opposite effects on the same physiological function, reducing the overall response. Here, the beta-blocker opposes the bronchodilatory effect of the beta-2 agonist, worsening bronchospasm.
questions.hint: Consider whether the drugs have opposite effects on the same physiological function.

questions.question: A dose-response curve for Drug Z is plotted in the presence and absence of a fixed concentration of Drug W. The curve shifts to the right without a change in the maximal response. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Drug W is a competitive antagonist.
options.explanation: A rightward shift in the dose-response curve with no change in the maximal response is characteristic of competitive antagonism.

options.text: Drug W is a non-competitive antagonist.
options.explanation: A non-competitive antagonist would reduce the maximal response without shifting the curve to the right.

options.text: Drug W is a chemical antagonist.
options.explanation: Chemical antagonism involves the formation of an inactive complex between two drugs, which is not reflected in a dose-response curve shift.

options.text: Drug W is an irreversible antagonist.
options.explanation: An irreversible antagonist would reduce the maximal response without shifting the curve to the right.

questions.explanation: A rightward shift in the dose-response curve with no change in the maximal response indicates that increasing concentrations of the agonist can overcome the antagonism. This is characteristic of competitive antagonism.
questions.hint: Consider the effect of the antagonist on the dose-response curve of the agonist.
